summary.name: Moving Past Shallow Incident Data
summary.one_liner: An essay arguing that shallow incident metrics such as MTTR, MTTD, and incident frequency reveal little about how teams actually handle incidents, and that deeper qualitative study is needed.
use_cases: Rethinking which incident metrics a team should track
Preparing for a deeper incident retrospective
Understanding limits of MTTR and MTTD averages
Studying how engineers handle uncertainty during outages
Building a case for qualitative incident analysis
summary.what_it_does: The essay walks through how a single incident duration becomes more data when detection time, dates, and multiple incidents are added, then argues that averages and charts of these numbers reveal little about team performance. It contends that incidents are dynamic, non-uniform events where people make decisions under time pressure and incomplete information, so central tendency metrics obscure more than they show. It proposes deeper questions to ask instead, such as how engineers share knowledge, improvise tools, decide when to call for help, and handle tradeoffs. It lists real incident patterns (late detection, shifting severity, fixes that worsen problems) to illustrate the mess that shallow data hides. It is a blog post by Adaptive Capacity Labs and cites two theses by Allspaw and Branlat.
notable: Argues that MTTR, MTTD and similar averages give little insight into incidents
Lists concrete deeper questions about knowledge sharing, improvisation, and escalation during incidents
Written by Adaptive Capacity Labs, citing Allspaw (2015) and Branlat (2011) research
caveats: This is an opinion essay, not a tool or product; it describes no software features
Offers no alternative metrics or methods in concrete detail beyond general qualitative questions
